# Null Distributions {#null-distributions}

<div class="draft">Work in progress.</div>

## How Far Is Far Enough?

- recap Chapter \@ref(t-statistic): ten scores about 1 SE from 49 (t = 0.95), nearly 4 SEs from 46 (t = 3.79)
- second feels more convincing, but how far is far enough?
- need: what t-values look like when there is no real difference (population mean = comparison value)
- define: null hypothesis; null distribution = spread of t-values when null true
- build it as in Chapter \@ref(standard-error): many samples, keep a result from each

<div class="summary-box">
sample -> group mean -> t-value -> repeat many times -> null distribution -> which values are rare?
</div>

<div class="note">
**What you need for this chapter**

- Chapters \@ref(functions) to \@ref(t-statistic) (up to one-sample t-test); not the rest of Part I
</div>

## A World Where The Null Is True

- real research: never know if null true; simulation: make it true on purpose
- made-up question: are people called Steve taller than average? world where they are not
- everyone: mean 175 cm, SD 7 cm; Steves exactly the same (made up, realistic for adults)

```{r steve-world, fig.cap="Left: in this world, the heights of people called Steve (dashed) match everyone's heights (filled) exactly. Right: a random sample of 10 Steves from that world. The heights are made up but realistic.", fig.alt="Two panels with height in centimetres on the x-axis. On the left, a filled normal curve for everyone and a dashed curve for people called Steve lie exactly on top of each other, centred on a dotted line at 175. On the right, ten dots for a sample of Steves, with a dotted line at 175 and a solid orange line at the sample mean of 179, about 4 cm higher.", echo=FALSE}
set.seed(4)
steves <- tibble(
  height = rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7),
  y = 1:10,
  panel = "Our sample"
)

world <- tibble(height = seq(150, 200, by = 0.5)) %>%
  mutate(density = dnorm(height, mean = 175, sd = 7), panel = "The world")

mean_lines <- tibble(
  panel = c("The world", "Our sample", "Our sample"),
  height = c(175, 175, mean(steves$height)),
  line = c("average", "average", "sample mean")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = world, aes(x = height, y = density, fill = "Everyone"),
            alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = world, aes(x = height, y = density,
                              colour = "People called Steve"),
            linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = steves, aes(x = height, y = y),
             size = 3, colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_vline(data = mean_lines, aes(xintercept = height, linetype = line),
             colour = c("grey20", "grey20", "#D55E00"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(panel, levels = c("The world", "Our sample")),
             scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c("Everyone" = "#467AAC")) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("People called Steve" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = c("average" = "dotted",
                                         "sample mean" = "solid")) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(order = 1),
    colour = guide_legend(order = 2),
    linetype = guide_legend(
      order = 3, override.aes = list(colour = c("grey20", "#D55E00"))
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"))
```

```{r steve-world-code, ref.label="steve-world", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

```{r steve-world-reset, include=FALSE}
# put the random numbers back where they were, so the rest of the chapter
# is not affected by the Steve example
set.seed(123)
```

- null here = Steves exactly average, no difference
- but sample of 10: mean `r round(mean(steves$height), 1)` cm, about `r round(mean(steves$height) - 175)` cm above average
- gap is purely which Steves ended up in the sample: sampling noise
- one-sample t-test compares sample mean with 175; question: how big a gap can noise alone produce?

- simulate the Steve world: `rnorm()` draws from a normal population (mean 175, SD 7), 10 Steves, t against 175

```{r one-null-sample}
null_sample <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)
null_sample

my_t_value(null_sample, comparison_value = 175)
```

- run a few times: heights and t change every time, though nothing is going on
- heights in cm; t = same comparison measured in SEs (t = 2: mean two SEs above 175)

```{r null-means-seed, include=FALSE}
# a fixed seed, so the numbers quoted below stay the same from render to render
set.seed(10)
```

```{r null-means}
null_means <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)))

c(sd_of_means = my_sd(null_means), formula_se = 7 / sqrt(10))
```

- means much tighter than individuals: SD 7 cm vs about `r round(my_sd(null_means), 1)` cm
- = SE from Chapter \@ref(standard-error), 7 / √10 = `r round(7 / sqrt(10), 2)` cm
- still some far from 175: tallest group `r round(max(null_means), 1)` cm, shortest `r round(min(null_means), 1)` cm, all from a world where Steves are average

  return(output)
}

my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)

`r hide("Show a hint")`
- `sample_values`: `rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)`; `output`: `my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)`
`r unhide()`

```{r my-null-t-solution}
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <- rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  output <- my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)
  return(output)
}

my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
```
`r unhide()`

## Check It Against R

- random, so different each run; `set.seed()` repeats the same random numbers
- same seed: `my_null_t()` should match `t.test()` on the same sample exactly

```{r my-null-t-check}
set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)

set.seed(1)
r_version <- unname(
  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)

c(mine = mine, R = r_version)
all.equal(mine, r_version)
```

## Many t-Values

- repeat 1000 times with `replicate()`

```{r null-ts}
null_ts <- replicate(1000, my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7))
```

```{r null-histogram, fig.cap="1000 t-values from groups of 10 Steves in a world where the null hypothesis is true.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 simulated t-values centred on zero, with most between -2 and 2 and a few further out in both tails.", echo=FALSE}
ggplot(tibble(t = null_ts), aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, colour = "white", fill = "#467AAC") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r null-histogram-code, ref.label="null-histogram", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- = null distribution of t for n = 10; each t = one group, in SEs not cm
- notice:
  - centred on 0 (on average sample mean = population mean)
  - most between about -2 and 2
  - a few further out, both directions, though null true
- point out: shape doesn't depend on population mean or SD, only n (any 10 values give same null distribution); next chapter relies on this

- which t-values common, which rare? widget: 1000 null t-values at a time
- slider picks rarest share, split across two tails

<iframe class="demyst-widget" src="apps/rareness/embed.html" width="100%" height="480" title="Which t-values are rare interactive widget" style="border: 0;"></iframe>

1. **Regenerate** a few times: details change, shape stays
2. move slider: orange = rarest; sentence under plot says where they start
3. how far from 0 before only rarest 5% left? same after regenerating?

## Where Do The Rare Values Start?

- put our `null_ts` in order: `sort()` smallest to largest; `head()` first six, `tail()` last six

```{r sorted-ts}
sorted_ts <- sort(null_ts)

head(sorted_ts)
tail(sorted_ts)
```

- rarest 5% of 1000 = 50, so 25 per tail
  - **lower cutoff**: 26th smallest (25 below)
  - **upper cutoff**: 975th (25 above, 1000 - 975 = 25)
- square brackets pick by position: `sorted_ts[1]` smallest, `sorted_ts[1000]` largest

### Your Turn: Write `my_cutoffs()`

- 26 and 975 only work for 1000 values and 5%; function generalises
- `alpha` = share marked rare (`0.05` = rarest 5%); explained properly next chapter
- steps: sort; count with `length()`; `k` = values per tail; lower at `k + 1`, upper at `n - k`

```{r my-cutoffs-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <-
  n <-
  k <-
  lower <-
  upper <-
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs(null_ts)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
- `sorted` = `sort(null_ts)`; `n` = `length(sorted)`
- `k` = `floor(n * alpha / 2)`; 1000 gives 25; `floor()` rounds down since positions are whole (990 gives 24.75, so 24)
- `lower` = `sorted[k + 1]`, `upper` = `sorted[n - k]`; with 1000, positions 26 and 975 as before
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-cutoffs-solution}
my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <- sort(null_ts)
  n <- length(sorted)
  k <- floor(n * alpha / 2)
  lower <- sorted[k + 1]
  upper <- sorted[n - k]
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs(null_ts)
```
`r unhide()`

- should match the by-position values
- note default `alpha = 0.05`, like defaults in Chapter \@ref(functions)

### See The Rare Values

- try `alpha_choice` = 0.5, 0.1, 0.05, 0.01
- orange = beyond cutoffs; dashed = cutoffs; table counts orange
- explain `|` = "or": `rare` TRUE below lower or above upper

```{r rare-plot, fig.cap="The null t-values, with the rarest 5% (alpha_choice = 0.05) in orange and dashed lines at the cutoffs.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 null t-values in blue, with the bars beyond about -2.1 and 2.2 coloured orange and dashed vertical lines at those two values."}
alpha_choice <- 0.05
rare_cutoffs <- my_cutoffs(null_ts, alpha = alpha_choice)

null_t_data <- tibble(t = null_ts) %>%
  mutate(rare = t < rare_cutoffs[1] | t > rare_cutoffs[2])

ggplot(null_t_data, aes(x = t, fill = rare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_cutoffs, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#467AAC", "TRUE" = "#D55E00"),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

null_t_data %>%
  summarise(beyond = sum(rare), share = mean(rare))
```

- at 0.05: exactly `r sum(null_t_data$rare)` of 1000 beyond, 25 per tail (by construction)
- smaller share: cutoffs move outwards

### Compare With R

- `qt()` = cutoffs for exact t distribution; n = 10 gives 9 df

```{r cutoffs-compare}
tibble(
  cutoff = c("lower", "upper"),
  simulated = my_cutoffs(null_ts),
  qt = qt(c(0.025, 0.975), df = 9)
)
```

- close, not identical: simulated cutoffs wobble with each new `null_ts`, like a sample mean

## Rare, But Not Impossible

- back to Steves: of 1000 means, only `r sum(null_means > 180)` above 180 cm, `r sum(null_means < 170)` below 170 cm
- top 2.5% (tallest 25) all above `r round(sort(null_means)[975], 1)` cm
- rare enough to make us wonder, but no believable reason for Steves to be taller, so fluke still better explanation
- contrast: group exposed to a toxin while growing up, comes out unusually short; equally rare
- difference is the alternative: toxin affecting growth is believable, so "something going on" beats fluke
- 5% of null t-values still past the cutoffs: 100 average first names, about 5 look unusual from noise alone

```{r my-functions-after-2a-null-distributions, eval=FALSE}
# Null Distributions -------------------------------------------------------
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <- rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  output <- my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <- sort(null_ts)
  n <- length(sorted)
  k <- floor(n * alpha / 2)
  lower <- sorted[k + 1]
  upper <- sorted[n - k]
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}
```
The rest of your file depends on which chapters you have done so far.
`r unhide()`

Then check that the saved file works on its own. This is the last chunk of the exercise file:

```{r toolbox-saved-check, eval=FALSE}
rm(list = ls())
source("my_functions.R")

set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
set.seed(1)
r_version <- unname(
  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)
all.equal(mine, r_version)

# 20:1 counts down from 20 to 1; with alpha = 0.1, one value is in each tail
all.equal(my_cutoffs(20:1, alpha = 0.1), c(2, 19))
```

You should see two `TRUE`s:

```text
[1] TRUE
[1] TRUE
```
